clinicalPearls: Primary hyperoxaluria is a group of inherited disorders of glyoxylate metabolism that cause marked overproduction of oxalate by the liver
It typically presents with recurrent calcium oxalate kidney stones and nephrocalcinosis, often from childhood, and can progress to renal failure
Type 1, from deficiency of the hepatic enzyme alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase, is the most common and generally the most severe form
As renal function declines, oxalate can no longer be cleared and deposits throughout the body (systemic oxalosis), affecting bone, heart, retina, and vessels
The diagnosis should be considered in any patient with recurrent oxalate stones, especially with early onset, a family history, or nephrocalcinosis
Elevated urinary oxalate, genetic testing, and sometimes liver biopsy establish the diagnosis, and high fluid intake with crystallisation inhibitors is a supportive measure

A subset of type 1 disease responds biochemically to pyridoxine, and definitive treatment historically involved combined or sequential liver and kidney transplantation, with newer RNA-targeted therapies now available
reference.pathophysiology: Primary hyperoxaluria results from autosomal recessive defects in enzymes of hepatic glyoxylate detoxification. In type 1, deficiency of the peroxisomal enzyme alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase allows glyoxylate to be oxidised to oxalate; types 2 and 3 involve other enzymes in the same pathway. The liver overproduces oxalate, which the kidneys excrete in high amounts, promoting calcium oxalate crystallisation, stone formation, and nephrocalcinosis. Because oxalate is poorly cleared once renal function fails, it accumulates systemically and is deposited in multiple tissues as oxalosis.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic recurrent calcium oxalate stone disease
Other hereditary stone-forming disorders such as cystinuria
Distal renal tubular acidosis with nephrocalcinosis
additionalInvestigations: Plasma oxalate, particularly as renal function declines
Stone analysis confirming calcium oxalate composition
Renal imaging for stones and nephrocalcinosis
Genetic testing for the causative enzyme defect
Liver enzyme assay on biopsy in selected diagnostic uncertainty
Assessment for systemic oxalosis when renal failure is present
redFlags: Progressive decline in renal function toward end-stage disease
Systemic oxalosis with cardiac, skeletal, retinal, or vascular involvement
Recurrent obstructing stones with infection or acute kidney injury
Early-onset stone disease with nephrocalcinosis suggesting a severe genotype
reference.prognosis: The outlook varies with type and genotype; type 1 disease can progress to end-stage renal failure and life-threatening systemic oxalosis, whereas some pyridoxine-responsive and non-type-1 forms are milder, and early diagnosis with modern therapies has improved outcomes considerably.
pitfalls: Treating recurrent stones symptomatically without recognising an underlying inherited metabolic cause
Confusing primary with enteric hyperoxaluria, which have different mechanisms and management
Overlooking systemic oxalosis as renal function falls
Performing isolated kidney transplantation in type 1 disease without addressing continued hepatic oxalate overproduction
management: Vigorous maintenance hyperhydration to lower urinary calcium oxalate supersaturation
Crystallisation inhibitors such as potassium citrate, orthophosphate and magnesium to reduce stone formation
Supervised pyridoxine (vitamin B6) trial, which is effective in a subset of type 1 disease
RNA-interference therapy directed at hepatic oxalate production, such as lumasiran, in type 1 disease
Stone clearance by lithotripsy or endourological removal, minimising nephron-damaging interventions
Monitoring of renal function and of urinary and plasma oxalate, with surveillance for systemic oxalosis affecting bone, heart, retina and vessels once renal function declines
Intensive dialysis and combined or sequential liver-kidney transplantation for type 1 disease progressing to end-stage renal failure
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance
